CZE.head: Czech players with 450+ minutes in the Big-5 leagues: 26 at the 2007/08 peak, 10 in 2025/26.
CZE.body:
The change-point model’s most probable season for the fall is 2014/15 (posterior 57 %), a level change of ×0.59 (90 % HDI 0.39–1.02); that interval includes ×1.00, so the fall is not distinguishable from no change at the 90 % level. Its most probable season for the other step, a rise, is 2000/01 (posterior 56 %), ×1.67 (90 % HDI 0.70–2.32); that interval includes ×1.00. A break model dates a change in level; it identifies no cause.

The median age of the nation’s Big-5 players was 28 at the 2007/08 peak and 32 in 2014/15, when no player made a first Big-5 season of 450+ minutes.

CZE.head: The per-head gap to Norway and Denmark, split over three measured channels (descriptive).
CZE.body:
In a ridge fit over 8 countries, against Norway (a gap of 6.98 per million) youth minutes go with +4.22 (90 % bootstrap interval +1.22 to +5.91), league strength with +5.12 (+1.90 to +6.77) and export age with 0.00, residual −2.37; against Denmark (a gap of 10.19 per million) youth minutes go with +7.35 (90 % bootstrap interval +2.17 to +10.27), league strength with +1.67 (+0.65 to +2.26) and export age with 0.00, residual +1.17.

The league-strength coefficient in this fit is negative (−56.5 per unit of the league multiplier): a weaker home league goes with more players in the top-ranked leagues per million, so a peer whose league is weaker than Czechia’s (m_L 0.665) gets a positive league-strength contribution. The export-age channel is zero by construction: Czechia, Norway and Denmark share the same median age at the first top-9 season among recent entrants (22). The split describes an association across few, correlated national measures; it is not a causal accounting.

CZE.head: Czechia’s own under-21 nationals’ share of home-league minutes over 6 seasons: a trend of −0.39 pp a season (90 % CI −1.26 to +0.48).
CZE.body: The share by season, 2020/21 to 2025/26: 10.3, 8.6, 9.0, 7.9, 11.1, 6.4 %. An OLS line through the 6 seasons falls by 0.39 percentage points a season (90 % CI −1.26 to +0.48 pp), an interval that includes zero. The last season’s share is a floor (FBref leaves part of the league’s rows without a nationality): at its ceiling of 7.6 % the slope is −0.21 pp a season (90 % CI −0.95 to +0.54). The last step, 2024/25 to 2025/26, for the comparison countries and for other leagues whose share fell by 2 points or more: Norway 10.5 → 11.5 %; Denmark 13.2 → 15.3 %; Poland 12.5 → 9.3 %; Spain 7.8 → 4.8 %.

CZE.head: Where Czechia ranks among 9 countries on the pathway measures, 2025/26 (1 = highest share, youngest age, most moves).
CZE.body: Under-21 share of home-league minutes 6.4 % (a floor; up to 7.6 %), 8 of 8 (highest: Denmark 15.3 %); regular under-21 starters per club 1.06, 8 of 8 (highest: Denmark 2.50); median age at the first season with real playing time abroad 24 (n = 32), 5–7 of 9 from youngest (youngest: Norway 22.5); first moves abroad in the covered seasons 32, 8 of 9 (most: Denmark 112); home-league UEFA-coefficient multiplier ×0.43, 2 of 9; median share of club minutes for exports 50 % (90 % bootstrap interval 22–66 %, n = 26), 3 of 9 by the median; 54 % of the 48 players who went from the home league to a top-9 league since 2020/21 left from Sparta Prague or Slavia Prague. These are descriptive ranks on medians and counts; apart from the minutes share they carry no interval, so neighbouring ranks can swap with a few players; none of them is shown to cause the per-head count.

CZE.head: Youth minutes in Germany and England after two academy reforms (descriptive).
CZE.body: Germany after its DFB/DFL academy licensing (2001/02; Honigstein, 2015): its own under-21 nationals played 5 % of Bundesliga minutes the season before, 11 % at the highest point within twelve seasons (2009/10) and 6 % in 2025/26. England after its Elite Player Performance Plan (2012/13; Premier League, 2011): its own under-21 nationals played 3 % of Premier League minutes the season before, 6 % at the highest point within twelve seasons (2019/20) and 3 % in 2025/26. Each is one sequence in one country without a comparison group, so it describes timing and does not estimate an effect of either reform.
